Should we have a contingency plan?

To say that the introduction of a contingency plan is a game changer, might be a bit hyperbolic. Yet, the addition of a contingency plan would take us to a new dimension as Price Action traders.

So what is a contingency plan

A dictionary definition would be: a course of action to be followed if a preferred plan fails or an existing situation changes.

This valid CE (long) leads us to our preferred plan- As we are in a Demand Zone, to enter on the buy side after the appearance of the CC. And then to ride price movement up using successively higher closing WRBs as profit targets, or as trailing stops, or using unfilled opposing Zones as profit targets. There is more to the plan of course, but for now we need only focus on "the riding price up" part.

Trading is about probabilities, not certainties. So there will be times, perhaps many times, when price does not go up, it goes down. This is why we always want to use a stop. But do we necessarily need our stop to be hit to know that our preferred plan is failing/has failed, or that the existing situation is changing/has changed? Obviously, we do not. So if we can use the available information to tell us we do not want to be long before our stop is hit, can we take that information one step further and deduce that the best course of action is to actually get short?

Before we delve into the rules of the contingency plan, we should note a few important things. First, before you can have a valid contingency plan entry, you must have a validCE. Second, we will be getting short in a Demand Zone and long in a Supply Zone. This is not the same thing as the zones "flipping" (more on this later).

Just a couple of nice charts.

One thing to not on the chart below. A Supply/Demand Delta Zone is not simply created by the appearance of a WRB. The WRB, along with some other requirements,must be a WRB Hidden GAP

Understanding the importance of Hidden GAPs naturally allows us to understand the importance of Actual GAPs. This Actual GAP was created as the new trading week began.

We all know the old adage, "Gaps are filled". Well, price shot away from this gap and finally made its way back up to it and filled it. While the gap was filled, the zone created was not closed. Nor was an entry signal necessarily triggered. Yet the zone was an obvious profit target for a long trade taken in the Demand zone below.

Chart two is just our basic CE long entry.

فقط چند نمودار قشنگ.

یک نکته در نمودار زیر: یک ناحیه دلتای عرضه/تقاضا صرفاً با ظاهر شدن یک WRB ساخته نمی‌شود. WRB، همراه با چند شرط دیگر، باید یک WRB Hidden GAP باشد.

درک اهمیت Hidden GAP‌ها طبیعتاً اجازه می‌دهد اهمیت Actual GAP‌ها را هم بفهمیم. این Actual GAP وقتی هفته معاملاتی جدید شروع شد ساخته شد.

همه ما این ضرب‌المثل قدیمی را می‌دانیم: «شکاف‌ها پر می‌شوند». خب، قیمت از این شکاف جهید و دور شد و در نهایت راهش را به بالا برگرداند و آن را پر کرد. با اینکه شکاف پر شد، ناحیه‌ای که ساخته شد بسته نشد. و لزوماً سیگنال ورودی هم فعال نشد. با این حال، آن ناحیه هدف سود واضحی برای یک معامله خرید در ناحیه تقاضای پایین‌تر بود.

نمودار دو فقط ورود ساده CE خرید ماست.

I came to RTM via Wyckoff and VSA.. as you may or may not remember from threads elsewhere. Now that I've internalized SD PA trading, I've taken volume off my charts because I found it unnecessary in trading successfully... For various reasons, which, what the heck, let's get into briefly:

1) VSAers get caught up with looking for high volume and miss a lot of trades. The market turns round on low, medium and high volume at different times. 2) NS/ND can be observed in real time by observing the candle being formed, you can see if there is high or low volume by the amount of activity and often the range/spread. When you see a succession of tiny bars, you know the volume was low, especially on a LTF. 3) On a LTF the volume doesn't seem necessary because it can be inferred from the candle with some degree of accuracy.. and on a HTF the tick volume profile tends to be rather flat. 4) If SD/PA is enough, then adding volume risks giving conflicting signals - if it aint broke, why fix it.

I'm sure there are other reasons, but those are some thoughts. My question is, for Forex trading, do you think there'd likely be much value in delving back into volume and VSA and trying to supercharge my trading with it, or do you think it would likely be unnecessary and a potential point of distraction and confusion?

Cheers man!

Hello ZeeDeveel and thank you for the question.

I have to be honest, I waffle back and forth on the use of volume all the time now. The only thing I know for sure, is that adding volume in another pane on the chart diminishes the amount of space available for PRICE.

You're right. From an entry signal standpoint, low volume is more important than high volume. Of course those with a deeper understanding of VSA would say, its that low volume occurring where once volume was high that is the real key.

If you like how things are going without volume, then there is no reason to add it to the mix. If you do add it, you will miss some trades you would have gotten before. However, the real key is, you will stay out of some bad trades you would have gotten into before.

In fact, many successful traders would argue that the question to ask about any new tool/methodology is not, "What will this get me in to?", but rather, "What will this keep me out of?".

I hope we can get some discussion going on this, because I am struggling with it myself.
